The New Britain naked-backed fruit bat (Dobsonia praedatrix) exhibits a suite of life-history traits that reflect a relatively slow pace of life for a pteropodid of its body size. Basal metabolic rate was measured in captive individuals under standard thermoneutral conditions at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], yielding a maximum oxygen consumption of 142.50 milliliters per hour [JOi = 142.50 milliliters per hour], a value that is consistent with the modest metabolic demands of a species inhabiting the stable, warm, lowland forests of the Bismarck Archipelago. Neonates emerge at a birth weight of 18.2 grams [Wwb = 18.2 grams], a value inferred from allometric relationships with the closely related Moluccan naked-backed fruit bat (Dobsonia moluccensis) and the species own estimated metabolic rate. This relatively small neonatal mass, approximately ten percent of the ultimate adult female body mass, is indicative of a reproductive strategy that prioritizes maternal mobility over extended in utero resource provisioning.

Female Dobsonia praedatrix reach a maximum adult body mass, or asymptotic wet weight, of 179.5 grams [Wwi = 179.5 grams], a figure that positions them as medium-sized members of their genus. This ultimate body size is achieved after a prolonged period of juvenile growth and is a key determinant of many downstream life-history parameters, from metabolic rate to reproductive output. Field records indicate that females produce one pup per litter [N_R_i = one pup per litter], with a single litter produced per year [F_R_i = single litter produced per year]. This annual reproductive event is tightly linked to the species stable thermal environment; at a body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], the energetic cost of gestation is considerable, and the production of a single, well-developed offspring annually represents an optimized trade-off between current and future reproductive success. The maximum longevity for Dobsonia praedatrix, based on data from its congener Dobsonia moluccensis, is estimated at approximately 10.1 years [am = approximately 10.1 years] under the physiological conditions typical of its active metabolic state at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This extended lifespan is characteristic of many island fruit bats and underscores a slow life-history strategy.

Gestation in Dobsonia praedatrix is a remarkably extended process, lasting approximately 150 days [tg = approximately 150 days] when the female maintains a core body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This gestational period, comparable to that of other medium-sized pteropodids, allows for the thorough development of a single precocial pup that is capable of clinging to its mother shortly after parturition. Following birth, the neonatal bat is entirely dependent on its mother for milk, entering a phase of intense maternal investment. The time since birth at weaning, when the young bat transitions to solid food and achieves nutritional independence, is estimated at 180 days since birth [tx = 180 days since birth], a duration that reflects the prolonged lactational period required to support the growth of a large-brained, slow-developing mammal at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This weaning period, occurring under a stable maternal body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], is followed by several months of independent juvenile life before the individual reaches sexual maturity.

Sexual maturity in Dobsonia praedatrix is not attained until a substantial period after weaning. The time since birth at puberty is estimated to be approximately 715 days since birth [tp = approximately 715 days since birth], meaning that a young bat born at the start of a breeding season is nearly two years old before its gonads become fully functional at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This delay allows for the continued skeletal growth and fat deposition necessary to reach the 179.5 grams [Wwi = 179.5 grams] adult female body mass. The pubertal transition, like all other metabolic processes in this homeothermic species, occurs under a core temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. The protracted juvenile phase is a common feature among pteropodid bats, which typically have low fecundity and high adult survival. In this species, the long interval between weaning and first reproduction also serves to reduce intraspecific competition for roosting and foraging resources within the dense island forests of its endemic range.

The foraging ecology of Dobsonia praedatrix, while not as well-studied as that of some Australian megabats, is thought to center on the consumption of native figs and other soft fruits typical of lowland tropical forests. These bats are important seed dispersers, and their relatively low daily energetic requirements, implied by the 142.50 milliliters per hour [JOi = 142.50 milliliters per hour] basal metabolic rate, allow them to subsist on a diet that may be seasonally variable at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C].
